title: Counting the Omer (Leviticus 23:15–16)
hookLine: forty-nine days counted from Passover to Shavuot

cards: After dark on the second night of Passover, someone stands, says a short blessing, and then says a number. Today is one day of the Omer. The next night, two days.
Then three. It goes on every night for seven weeks, out loud, a blessing and a number, until forty-nine. Nothing is crossed off, and nothing is skipped.
A sentence that takes ten seconds to say, and a household that has to remember it forty-nine nights in a row. And if someone forgets a night, there's a rule for that too.

teach.h: SEVEN WEEKS SHALL THERE BE COMPLETE.
teach.b: It comes from the Torah: "And ye shall count unto you" from the day the first sheaf of the harvest was brought to the priest, "seven weeks shall there be complete," and then the fiftieth day is a festival.

That first sheaf was the omer, a measure of grain, and it names the whole period: the Omer, and the practice, counting the Omer. Passover falls at the barley harvest; seven weeks later come the wheat harvest and Shavuot.
So the count ties two harvests together.
Over time, the rabbis also saw it tying two events together: leaving Egypt, and receiving the Torah at Sinai. Leaving slavery, then receiving a way to live. The count is the road between them.
The way it's done is precise.
Each night after dark, a blessing, then the number: today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer. You say it, not just think it, and you count up.

Forget one night, and you can count the next day, without the blessing. But miss a whole day, and the Shulchan Aruch rules that you keep counting every night, just without the blessing, because the chain was broken.
The weeks have a sadder side too.

Tradition remembers that many of Rabbi Akiva's students died in this season, so some communities keep signs of mourning, like no weddings, until the thirty-third day, Lag BaOmer, a day of bonfires and joy.
In kabbalah, each of the forty-nine days is linked to its own quality to work on, so each day is worth something by itself.

how: From the second night of Passover, many Jews count the Omer each night after dark: a blessing, then the day and week (today is twelve days, which is one week and five days of the Omer), for forty-nine nights until Shavuot.

games.q: it's the morning, and you realize you forgot to count the Omer last night. what do many authorities say to do?
o: give up the count for this year.
count now, during the day, without the blessing.
count two days tonight to catch up.
games.why: you can count during the day without the blessing, and go back to counting with the blessing that night.

practice: Count your breaths up, slowly, one to seven, and start again; there's no end to rush toward, and each breath is complete in itself. Then think of something you're in the middle of, and say to yourself what day of it this is.

wordCard.voice: Omer. A sheaf of barley, and the forty-nine days counted aloud, night by night, from Passover to Shavuot.

orig.note: Hebrew: a sheaf, a measure of grain; the barley offering brought on Passover.

carryVoice: Your line: count the days up. A habit, a recovery, a new job: every day of it is one more, not one less. That's day one hundred thirty-six.
